items.prompt: State what is meant by the rural-urban fringe.
items.canonical_answer: The zone at the edge of a city where urban and rural land uses meet: new housing estates and warehouses standing beside smallholdings, market gardens and open land that the city has not yet reached.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning of the term, the meeting zone of urban and rural land uses at the city's edge; accept named land uses from each side.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.6 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and give reasons for the characteristics of, and changes in, land use in urban areas

items.prompt: Explain why the tallest buildings in a city are usually found in the CBD.
items.canonical_answer: The CBD is the most accessible point for the whole urban area, so businesses compete to locate there, and their bidding pushes the land value to its highest point. Because each square metre of ground costs so much, whoever builds on it uses the air above it, so offices and shops stack into high-rise blocks, which is how the highest land values cause the tallest buildings. Because housing cannot pay those ground rents, it moves out and the CBD stays commercial.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3, each step a because-and-so: highest accessibility causes highest land values; so building upwards uses the costly ground most intensively; which means housing cannot afford the ground, so the CBD stays commercial and towers above the zones around it.

items.prompt:
The table shows land use by distance from the city centre, in one city:

| distance from centre | main land use | typical building height | open space |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 to 1 km | offices and major shops | 10 to 30 storeys | under 2 per cent |
| 1 to 4 km | older housing and small workshops | 2 to 4 storeys | 8 per cent |
| 4 to 10 km | newer housing estates | 1 to 2 storeys | 15 per cent |
| beyond 10 km | farms and new warehouses | 1 storey | over 60 per cent |

Describe the changes in land use shown with increasing distance from the centre.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows land use changing step by step outwards: the centre holds offices and major shops at 10 to 30 storeys, which gives way to older housing and workshops at 2 to 4 storeys, then to newer estates of 1 to 2 storeys, and finally to farms and warehouses. The values fall with distance: the buildings drop from 30 storeys to 1, and open space climbs from under 2 per cent to over 60. The pattern shown is the CBD, the inner city, the suburbs and the fringe in sequence, so the table means land values fall with distance from the centre and each zone uses the ground it can afford.
marking_guidance: Reading: the trend read from the table, land use changing zone by zone with distance (1 mark).

Values: the figures quoted, storeys falling from 10 to 30 at the centre to 1 beyond 10 km, and open space rising from under 2 per cent to over 60 per cent (1 mark); so the answer interprets the figures as falling land values outwards, which means the zones follow what each use can pay (1 mark).

items.prompt: A new out-of-town shopping centre with free parking has just opened beside the ring road. Suggest what may happen to land use in the city's CBD over the next ten years.
items.canonical_answer: This example suggests the CBD may lose part of its shopping trade, because customers who value free parking and one stop will follow the new centre, so some ground-floor shops may close or give way to other uses, such as cafes and offices. Because the upper floors were already struggling to pay high rents, some offices may also move out, so vacant buildings could spread, which means the CBD's land use may shift away from major retail towards services, eating and entertainment that the out-of-town centre cannot supply. Nothing here is fixed: a CBD that keeps its unique services may hold its trade.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used, the free parking and ring-road position of the new centre (1 mark).

Reasons: customers follow convenience, so ground-floor shops may close or change use (1 mark); therefore the CBD may shift towards uses the new centre cannot supply, so the change is suggested rather than certain (1 mark).

items.prompt: Asked to describe the land use of a city's CBD, a learner writes: 'The CBD is changing because online shopping is taking its customers away.' Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has answered a different question: the error is explaining why the CBD is changing when the question asks what its land use is. Describing the land use means naming what stands there now, high-rise offices, major shops and banks with little open space, so the description comes from reading the resource or the district itself. The reason for change belongs to an explain question, which is not the same task, so the answer should first describe and only then, if asked, explain.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named, an explanation of change given where the question asks for a description; the two tasks are not the same.
1 mark: the correct idea, the land use is described from what stands there, high offices, shops, banks, little open space, instead of reasons for change.

items.prompt: A council owns a car park on the edge of the CBD. A developer offers to build a 20-storey office block on it; a campaign wants it kept as the district's only public open space. Suggest which use the council should prefer, with reasons.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is that the office block is the better use, because of what the ground is worth. The plot sits at the CBD's edge, the most accessible district for the whole city, so land values there are high, and a 20-storey block uses them as no car park can; the rent the council earns can pay for public open space elsewhere, in districts where land is cheaper. The campaign's point is real, because open space in a dense district matters, but the evidence of land values suggests the same benefit costs less elsewhere, so the decision should trade the expensive ground for the cheaper and add to both.
marking_guidance: Judgement: 1 mark for a stated decision, the office block.
Because: 1 mark for the reasoning, the high land values of the CBD edge are used by the tower and wasted on tarmac, so the rent can buy open space where land is cheap.
Evidence: 1 mark for the figures or named values used, the 20 storeys on CBD-edge land against open space priced at fringe values, so the judgement is justified with evidence.

items.prompt:
The table shows a city's morning rush hour:

| mode | people moved per hour into the centre | road space per traveller |
|---|---|---|
| private car | 40 000 | large |
| bus | 55 000 | small |
| walking and cycling | 8 000 | smallest |

Suggest how the bus might help solve the city's congestion problem.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the answer working already: this resource shows buses move 55 000 people an hour into the centre, more than the cars' 40 000, while taking far less road space per traveller, because a bus carries dozens in the space of two or three cars. So a switch of even part of the car users to buses would move the same people on a fraction of the road space, which frees the streets for the buses themselves and for goods vehicles; because congestion follows the number of vehicles, not the number of people, moving people out of separate cars cuts it directly.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used, 55 000 people an hour by bus against 40 000 by car on far less road space (1 mark).
Reasons: buses carry dozens per vehicle, so road space per traveller is small (1 mark); therefore shifting car users onto buses cuts vehicle numbers, so the congestion eases (1 mark).

items.prompt: A fast-growing city cannot build homes fast enough for its new arrivals. One plan is to clear the informal settlements and build apartment blocks; a second is to upgrade them in place, adding water and toilets to the existing self-built houses. Suggest which plan the city should choose, with reasons.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is that upgrading is the better decision, because of what each plan does to people. Clearing removes the homes the arrivals have already built and rehouses only as fast as the city can build, which historically leaves families waiting years in worse conditions, so the shortage deepens while the blocks rise. Upgrading keeps the homes and the communities intact and adds what they lack, water points, toilets, storm drains, at a fraction of the cost per household, so the same budget reaches several times more families. The evidence is in the cost per household, so the better judgement is to upgrade first and rebuild later, provided land is not needed for a road or a flood line.
marking_guidance: Judgement: 1 mark for a stated decision, upgrading in place.
Because: 1 mark for the reasoning weighed, clearing destroys homes before replacements exist, while upgrading adds services at far lower cost per household, so the budget reaches more people.
Evidence: 1 mark for the figures or comparisons named, cost per household several times lower, so the decision rests on evidence.

items.prompt:
The table shows one city's growth against its housing:

| year | population | dwelling units | households sharing one water point |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2000 | 400 000 | 110 000 | 1 in 20 |
| 2010 | 720 000 | 168 000 | 1 in 8 |
| 2020 | 1 100 000 | 235 000 | 1 in 3 |

Describe the trend the table shows in housing and services.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows growth outrunning building: population nearly tripled from 400 000 in 2000 to 1 100 000 in 2020, but dwelling units only doubled, 110 000 to 235 000, so the gap between homes and households widened each decade. The water-point figures show the same trend on the service side: sharing rose from 1 household in 20 to 1 in 3, so by 2020 three times as many families stood at each standpipe as in 2000. The pattern shown is arrivals outnumbering both homes and pipes, which means the housing shortage and service pressure are two readings of one cause, growth.
marking_guidance: Reading: the trend read from the table, population growing faster than homes or services (1 mark).

Values: the figures quoted, 400 000 to 1 100 000 people against 110 000 to 235 000 homes, and sharing rising from 1 in 20 to 1 in 3 (1 mark); so the answer links the two readings to one cause, which means the figures support the conclusion (1 mark).

items.prompt: Asked how a named city has tried to solve its housing shortage, a learner writes: 'Build more houses, provide services, improve transport and create jobs.' Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is that the answer is a generic list with no place detail, so it could be about any city, which means it answers the question about none. A case-study answer names the city and its schemes and says how each works: for Windhoek, the mass-housing and serviced-land programmes launched from 2014, which prepare plots with water and power before settlement arrives, and the Shack Dwellers Federation of Namibia, whose saving schemes have helped thousands of families secure land and build at well below market cost. The test is whether the answer could be about any city; if it could, it is not yet about the one asked for.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named, a generic list with no place detail, which fits any city and so names none.
1 mark: the correct idea, a case-study answer names the city and its schemes, such as Windhoek's serviced-land programme and the Shack Dwellers Federation, instead of a bare list.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.6 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Explain the problems of urban areas, their causes and possible solutions

items.prompt: Asked to explain how better public transport could reduce traffic congestion in one city, a learner writes: 'Buses are cheaper than cars and they are better for the environment, and anyway the real problem is crime.' Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has left the question's subject: cost and environmental benefit are other problems' arguments, and crime is a different problem altogether, whereas the question asks how public transport reduces congestion. The correct idea keeps to the mechanism asked for: a bus carries dozens of people in the road space of two or three cars, so shifting drivers onto buses cuts the number of vehicles converging on the centre, which is how congestion eases. The test is whether every point is about the problem the question names, and here only congestion counts.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named, the answer argues cost, environment and crime instead of the congestion mechanism the question asks for.
1 mark: the correct idea, kept to the problem named: buses move the same people in fewer vehicles, so congestion falls, instead of other problems.

items.prompt: For Windhoek, describe two features of its urban land use.
items.canonical_answer: The CBD runs along Independence Avenue, with the city's high-rise offices, its major shops and banks standing where land values are highest. To the north-west lies Katutura, the older, denser suburb of small houses laid out in the 1960s, while the fast-growing informal settlements, Havana and Okahandja Park among them, spread across the northern fringe where arrivals build for themselves.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: the CBD of offices and high-rise shops; the dense older suburb and the fringe settlements against it.
Each feature is a fact of the named city, Windhoek, not a general point about land use.

items.prompt: For Windhoek, explain how the city has tried to solve the problems of its fast-growing informal settlements.
items.canonical_answer: Windhoek's northern settlements, Havana and Okahandja Park among them, grew faster than services could follow, so this example shows causes answered with named schemes. The mass-housing and serviced-land programmes, launched from 2014, prepare plots with water, roads and power before settlement arrives, because servicing land first means new housing starts with the pipes already in the ground. The Shack Dwellers Federation of Namibia organises saving groups, and since the 1990s it has helped thousands of families secure land and build homes at well below market cost, because self-help building turns the residents' own labour into houses the market would not supply. Together the schemes attack the shortage from both ends, so the city adds services and the residents add rooms.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 4, each point from the named example: the settlements outgrew the services, so the problem is stated; the serviced-land programme prepares water and power first, which means pipes arrive before houses; the Federation's saving groups build at well below market cost, so residents' labour supplies homes; therefore the two together add both services and rooms, which is how the shortage is answered.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.6 claim ledger.
objective_titles: A case study of an urban area or urban areas

items.prompt: For a named urban area you have studied, describe the problems of its growth and explain how far the solutions tried have succeeded. [7]
items.canonical_answer: Windhoek, Namibia's capital of about 486 000 people (2023), grew faster than its services. The northern informal settlements, Havana and Okahandja Park among them, took arrivals faster than water and sewerage followed, so households shared standpipes between many families and taxis queued on unsurfaced streets, and the CBD's traffic thickened as car ownership rose. The city's answers are specific. The mass-housing and serviced-land programmes, launched from 2014, prepare plots with water, roads and power before settlement arrives, which turns new growth from a problem into a serviced process. The Shack Dwellers Federation of Namibia, through saving groups running since the 1990s, has helped thousands of families secure land and build at well below market cost. The southern bypass takes through-traffic out of the CBD, and the MoveWindhoek plan of the 2010s proposes bus rapid transit for the rest. The judgement is that the solutions have partly succeeded: serviced land has reached thousands of plots and the Federation thousands of homes, but the settlements keep growing, so the schemes trail the need and the backlog persists.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about city problems, with no named example or only general points.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named urban area, capped at 5 if no named example is given.

Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail, Windhoek, Havana and Okahandja Park, the 2014 serviced-land programme, the Shack Dwellers Federation, the bypass, covering the problems, the solutions and a judgement of how far they have succeeded.

items.prompt:
The table shows land use in one district of a city that has grown from 200 000 people in 1990 to 650 000 in 2020:

| land use | share of district land, 1990 | share of district land, 2020 |
|---|---|---|
| offices and major shops | 18 per cent | 31 per cent |
| housing | 54 per cent | 43 per cent |
| industry and warehousing | 12 per cent | 9 per cent |
| farmland and open land | 16 per cent | 17 per cent |

(a) Identify the land use with the largest share of the district in 1990. [1]
(b) Describe two changes in land use between 1990 and 2020 shown by the table. [2]
(c) Suggest reasons for the growth of the offices and major shops share. [3]
(d) Suggest one problem the district's growth may have caused and how the city could reduce it. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Housing.
(b) Offices and major shops grew from 18 per cent to 31 per cent of the district, and housing fell from 54 per cent to 43 per cent, so commercial land use grew at housing's expense.
(c) The city more than tripled, from 200 000 to 650 000 people, so more customers and firms compete for the most accessible district, which pushes its land values up; and commercial uses outbid housing for that ground, which is why the office share grows. The district may also have added higher buildings over the same years, using the ground more intensively.
(d) Traffic congestion: many more trips now converge on the same district streets. The city could add bus priority lanes, so more people travel per road space and vehicle numbers fall.
marking_guidance: Resource: (a) 1 mark for the land use read from the table, housing at 54 per cent.
Marks and figures: (b) 2 marks, 1 per change with the values, the rise of offices from 18 to 31 per cent and the fall of housing from 54 to 43 per cent.
Evidence: (c) 3 marks, the population figures used (1), the land-value mechanism, commercial outbidding housing (1), and the intensification of building (1).
Problem and answer: (d) 2 marks, congestion named from the evidence (1), so a solution such as bus priority with its mechanism (1).
